routes.description: Establish the nature and commands of God as a unified foundation for objective moral value and obligation, then show that this account explains the relevant moral phenomena with fewer or less serious foundational difficulties than godless normative realism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine nature supplies a nonarbitrary standard of goodness, divine authority constitutes universally applicable duties, and the resulting account retains a comparative explanatory advantage over irreducible godless normativity.

motionBridge.description: Connect God's necessarily good nature and authoritative commands to a comparatively adequate account of both objective moral values and objective duties.

centralBridges.description: Explain why God's essential nature can constitute the paradigm of moral goodness without appealing to an independent moral standard.
Explain how commands consistent with God's nature generate genuine obligations while allowing derivative principles and morally relevant circumstances to govern particular cases.
Show that the rival account's irreducible moral entities and natural-to-moral relations lack sufficient metaphysical or explanatory support.
Preserve responsible agency and moral knowledge under the theistic account while identifying whether the rival naturalistic setting can support both.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for how divine moral requirements bind agents who do not explicitly identify God as their source, including difficult cases of impaired moral understanding.
Explain the role of general divine commands in responsibility, recognition of wrongdoing, and accountability despite anticipated disobedience.

routes.description: Establish irreducible normative facts and morally relevant nondivine features as sufficient grounds for objective value and obligation, then show that appeals to God neither uniquely explain those facts nor avoid comparable explanatory stopping points.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if godless normative realism accounts for objective goodness, duties, agency, and moral knowledge while the proposed theistic foundation proves unnecessary or rests on equally basic normative assumptions.

motionBridge.description: Connect irreducible moral facts and morally relevant features of situations to a complete, nondivine account of objective moral values and duties.

centralBridges.description: Explain how intrinsic values and irreducible normative relations can be basic features of reality and can ground obligations without divine commands.
Show that suffering, promises, capacities, and other morally relevant facts can generate duties without requiring an additional divine order.
Establish that theistic grounding also terminates in normative assumptions or unexplained relations, preventing obscurity objections from yielding a comparative advantage.
Provide a godless account compatible with responsible mental causation and justified confidence in evolved cognitive and moral faculties.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether commands can bind agents who do not apprehend their source or authority and whether the theory treats impaired agents consistently.
Determine whether divine commands add a necessary normative function beyond communicating existing good and evil, especially when disobedience is anticipated.

sections.title: Ultimate Ground of Moral Value
sections.rationale: The competing accounts must identify what makes goodness and badness objective: God's essential nature or irreducible normative features. This issue also tests whether either proposed standard imports an unexplained normative premise.

sections.title: Constitution and Scope of Objective Duty
sections.rationale: The motion expressly includes duties, making the dispute between authoritative divine commands and obligations generated by morally relevant nondivine facts a principal burden for both sides.

sections.title: Metaphysical Relations and Explanatory Ultimates
sections.rationale: Both routes depend on foundational relations linking their proposed grounds to moral facts. The comparative burden includes ontology, causal or constitutive intelligibility, theoretical economy, and the legitimacy of explanatory stopping points.

sections.title: Universality, Accountability, and the Purpose of Commands
sections.rationale: An account of duty must explain who is bound, how authority reaches unaware or impaired agents, why commands are needed, and how wrongdoing and accountability arise when commands are violated.

sections.title: Moral Agency and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Objective duties require agents capable of responsible action, while objective moral claims require defensible epistemic access. The rival accounts therefore must support freedom, mental efficacy, and reliable moral cognition.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God's necessarily good character grounds objective moral values, while divine commands consistent with that character constitute objective moral duties.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person opening speech remains Craig's, with explicit references to the theistic view he is defending.

response.rationale: This is a constructive statement of the theistic route, so no earlier opposing move supplies a response demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly and compactly establishes both proposed halves of the theistic account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between values grounded in character and duties constituted by commands is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The foundational thesis is asserted categorically, while the excerpt gives the account more clearly than it proves its comparative adequacy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two-part grounding account is internally consistent, though the authority-to-obligation bridge remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt explains the proposed constitution relation but offers limited defense of why divine commands generate obligations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states the motion-level foundation for both objective values and objective duties.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its own positive account and does not materially interpret a live rival alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly grounds values in God's character and duties in commands constrained by that character.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Godless normative realism is less plausible than theism because its independently real abstract moral objects add an extravagant ontology without sufficient support.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig names Wielenberg's view, describes its alleged Platonism, and contrasts it throughout with his own theistic account.

response.rationale: This is a constructive comparative objection to godless realism and has no earlier opposing response target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly advances a central metaphysical objection, though its supporting presumption is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition is recoverable, but the relevant sense of ontological extravagance is only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The stated presumption supplies some comparative force, but the excerpt does not fully defend why abstract ontology is disfavored.

charity.alternative: Abstract moral entities may be theoretically justified by their explanatory contribution despite ontological cost.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt invokes a presumption against Platonism without comparing that contribution in detail.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from added abstract ontology to reduced plausibility is usable but depends on an underdefended simplicity premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The metaphysical presumption is asserted rather than supported through representative comparison or independent argument.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks a central bridge concerning the rival account's metaphysical and explanatory support.

representationalCharity.rationale: The rival can answer through explanatory indispensability, an alternative the objection does not seriously examine here.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts abstract moral objects with a concrete divine ground and calls the former metaphysically extravagant.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The proposed causal connection between physical situations and abstract moral properties is obscure because abstract objects appear unable to enter causal relations with physical reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted Craig speech explicitly attributes the causal-supervenience proposal to Wielenberg and repeatedly evaluates it.

response.rationale: This constructive objection challenges the rival's relation between physical situations and moral properties without a reply target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies a definite central explanatory demand concerning the natural-to-moral relation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is recoverable, but it moves between supervenience and causal connection without fully distinguishing them.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the relation unintelligible outruns the excerpt because supervenience need not itself be a causal relation.

charity.alternative: Moral properties may supervene noncausally on physical facts through a necessary normative relation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt frames the relation causally and does not address this noncausal interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge identifies a real explanatory question but substantially risks equivocating between causation and supervenience.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim of unintelligibility rests mainly on the asserted causal incapacity of abstract objects.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central bridge requiring support for natural-to-moral relations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection materially weakens the strongest rival account by treating supervenience as though it must be causal.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls moral-property supervenience unintelligible and asks how abstract goodness or badness relates to physical situations.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Defining obligation by decisive moral reasons mishandles supererogation, tends to require the morally best act, and supplies only a conditional reason to act morally rather than an unconditional duty.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly labels this his second objection and directly describes and criticizes Wielenberg's account of moral obligation.

response.rationale: This constructive attack tests whether the rival's decisive-reasons account can distinguish obligation from moral desirability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely identifies supererogation and unconditional authority as decisive duty-account demands.

precisionFindings.rationale: The examples and conditional-duty conclusion make the objection's terms, scope, and inferential demand explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples warrant pressure on the theory, but the conditional-reason conclusion assumes an undefended desire-based reading of reasons.

charity.alternative: Decisive moral reasons can be categorical and can coexist with permissions excluding supererogatory acts from obligation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt does not address categorical reasons or exclusionary permissions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The supererogation challenge is coherent, but the move from decisive reasons to merely conditional obligation needs a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete examples support the distinction, while the general claim about conditional reasons remains insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the rival's central account of how nondivine normative facts generate duties.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly raises the issue but omits two important resources available to the rival account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts better acts with obligatory acts and argues that decisive reasons yield at most a conditional ought.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Physical causal closure and a self reduced to successive mental states eliminate free agency and an enduring moral agent, thereby undermining genuine accountability.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly identifies Wielenberg's commitments and traces their alleged implications for minds, selves, freedom, and accountability.

response.rationale: This constructive objection attacks the rival route's capacity to preserve mental efficacy, freedom, and continuing agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly engages the central agency bridge, though several metaphysical steps are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but closure, physical causation, mental efficacy, and personal endurance are run together.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Closure alone does not entail epiphenomenalism or the absence of an enduring agent without additional identity premises.

charity.alternative: Mental states may be physically realized and causally efficacious under physical closure, with agency persisting through realization.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection does not exclude identity or realization accounts of mental causation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion depends on unsupported transitions from closure to mental impotence and from mental succession to no enduring agent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt states consequences of closure but provides little support for the necessary anti-physicalist premises.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the rival's central burden to preserve responsible agency under naturalism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument targets a dualist reading of closure and omits a decisive physicalist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says physical closure makes mental states causally impotent and uses that claim to undermine freedom and accountability.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Naturalism joined to unguided evolution undercuts confidence in reliable moral cognition, whereas theism can ground reliable cognitive faculties through divine supervision of evolution.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig announces a third objection, invokes Plantinga's evolutionary argument, and applies it explicitly to Wielenberg's naturalistic moral epistemology.

response.rationale: This constructive objection challenges whether naturalism and unguided evolution permit justified confidence in moral cognition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly raises the central epistemic reliability demand and offers a contrasting theistic mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The defeater thesis is clear, but its scope shifts from cognition generally to moral cognition without a full distinction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical defeater claim needs probability and conditionalization arguments not supplied in the selected excerpt.

charity.alternative: Selection for adaptive behavior may correlate sufficiently with broadly reliable cognition, supplemented by observation and correction.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt does not compare this reliability pathway with the asserted divine guarantee.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed defeater is intelligible, but the inference from unguided selection to epistemic defeat is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt asserts unreliability pressure and divine supervision without supplying comparative probabilities or independent evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central agency-and-epistemology bridge of the godless route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection presents its skeptical conclusion without seriously handling an important evolutionary reliability alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts an alleged naturalistic defeater with the possibility of divinely supervised evolutionary reliability.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Suffering is intrinsically bad, while morally relevant features of a situation can generate obligations as irreducible features of reality without dependence on God.
moves.attributionBasis: A new speaker greets Craig, introduces the child-on-fire example, contrasts his view with Craig's, and states his own theory in first person.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the core godless account of intrinsic badness and situation-grounded obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly advances both objective value and objective duty components of the godless route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The child-suffering example clearly separates intrinsic badness from the facts giving rise to an obligation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The example makes the view intelligible, but it illustrates rather than independently establishes irreducible normative relations.

charity.alternative: The suffering and surrounding facts may be morally relevant while still requiring divine authority to constitute obligation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move asserts that these facts give rise to duty but does not independently exclude the authority requirement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The intrinsic-value and obligation claims form a consistent basic-fact account, with one compressed grounding bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The vivid example supports intuitive plausibility but does not fully defend the claimed irreducibility or sufficiency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the motion-level nondivine foundation for values and duties.

representationalCharity.rationale: The theistic alternative is acknowledged by analogy, although its distinct account of obligation remains underaddressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt treats suffering as bad in itself and the suffering, available water, and circumstances as generating obligation.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Objections alleging obscure causal relations and unexplained necessary moral connections have corresponding force against the theistic account and therefore establish no comparative advantage.
moves.attributionBasis: Wielenberg states his comparative method and then explicitly mirrors Craig's objections against divine causation, commands, and necessary divine goodness.

components.text: Show why the alleged obscurity of the natural-to-moral relation creates a comparative disadvantage rather than a shared stopping point.
Establish that the rival's metaphysical costs are not matched by corresponding unexplained commitments in the theistic view.

response.rationale: The parity strategy contacts the comparative inference by arguing that corresponding objections apply to theism, although the selected excerpt only begins the examples.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative component but leaves the detailed correspondence substantially compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cancellation thesis is clear, though the scope of which objections are genuinely corresponding remains underdeveloped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker uses qualified language and frames parity as a consideration rather than a conclusive demonstration.

charity.alternative: Theistic and godless stopping points may differ in ontological cost, explanatory role, or intelligibility despite surface symmetry.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt states correspondence without yet showing equality along those comparative dimensions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Matched objections can defeat a comparative inference, but actual cancellation requires an additional equivalence argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The strategy is clearly stated, while the selected evidence offers only the beginning of a representative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central realist-challenge bridge by denying comparative advantage.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the actual comparative issue but does not fully address potentially decisive asymmetries.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly proposes testing Craig's objections for corresponding theistic objections and says many appear matched.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Physical causal closure does not exclude mental causation unless one adds the contentious premise that mental states cannot also be physical states.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person response explicitly identifies Craig's allegation and develops Wielenberg's physicalist answer to it.

components.text: Determine whether physical causal closure itself entails that mental states are causally impotent and agency is eliminated.

response.rationale: The reply identifies a missing premise—no mental state is physical—and states that closure alone cannot yield Craig's causal-impotence conclusion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly diagnoses the missing premise at the decisive inference and explains the defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Closure, the disputed implication, and the required identity premise are distinctly and explicitly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited logical claim—that the conclusion requires an additional premise—is proportionate to the stated analysis.

charity.alternative: Craig may supplement closure with an independent argument that mental properties cannot be identical with physical properties.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply establishes only that closure by itself is insufficient, not that every supplemented argument fails.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The missing-premise diagnosis is explicit, valid, and directly defeats the claimed implication from closure alone.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual analysis is well supported by the stated formulation, with only the broader mind-body debate left open.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central agency objection and preserves a path for rival agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately limits its rebuttal to the inference actually presented while recognizing where further argument could enter.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes the closure principle and identifies the further premise needed to infer mental causal impotence.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Godless normative realism can accommodate supererogatory action through exclusionary permissions, while Christian love commands may render the proposed theistic examples obligatory.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker names Craig's supererogation objection, answers it in two expressly numbered stages, and closes by denying any comparative advantage.

components.text: Explain how godless normative realism can preserve genuinely supererogatory action rather than requiring every morally best act.
Assess whether the theistic command account itself clearly permits the proposed acts to remain above obligation.

response.rationale: The move contacts the decisive supererogation demand through exclusionary permissions and also turns the example against Christian commands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the central supererogation challenge, though the selected excerpt only begins the positive permission mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-part response is recoverable, though generic theism and specifically Christian commands are not always kept separate.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly marks uncertainty and offers the Christian-command point as a qualified challenge.

charity.alternative: A generic divine-command theory may allow permissions even if a particular Christian interpretation imposes demanding love duties.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply acknowledges generic theism but partly relies on Craig's Christian commitments for its reversal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Exclusionary permissions coherently answer the objection, while the Christian-theism reversal is a distinct conditional argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The response identifies plausible theoretical resources but only partially develops their operation in the selected evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the rival account's central capacity to distinguish duty from supererogation.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly notes the generic-versus-Christian distinction, though the reversal remains dependent on the latter interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt addresses Craig's sacrifice and career examples, questions their status under Christian love commands, and introduces two replies.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Divine commands are not the unique source of obligation because promises, preventable suffering, and other morally relevant features can themselves generate genuine duties.
moves.attributionBasis: Wielenberg announces challenges to Craig's account and develops the first through the child-in-flames case and an extended promise-only analogy.

components.text: Show whether divine commands are required as the constitutive and ultimate source of every objective moral obligation.
Explain how morally relevant nondivine facts can generate obligations rather than merely conditional moral recommendations.

response.rationale: The move directly denies uniqueness and offers promises and preventable suffering as alternative obligation-generating features.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive necessity claim with multiple counterexamples, though the grounding relation remains basic.

precisionFindings.rationale: The uniqueness claim, proposed alternatives, and contrast between the two theories are all clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support plural relevance, but their capacity to generate duties without further authority is not independently demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Promises and suffering may specify command-governed duties without themselves constituting the ultimate source of obligation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move treats their moral relevance as sufficient to establish their independent source status.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample strategy is coherent, though it needs a bridge from morally relevant feature to independent duty source.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Promises and preventable suffering provide intuitive support but do not settle the disputed constitutive relation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the rival's central command-nonnecessity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It engages the hierarchy issue but underaddresses the distinction between ultimate and derivative sources.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names promises, needless preventable suffering, divine commands, and other factors as genuine sources of obligation.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Commands cannot bind agents who apprehend neither their content nor the commander's authority, leaving divine-command theory unable to ground obligations for unaware nonbelievers.
moves.attributionBasis: The expressly introduced second challenge is delivered continuously through parental examples and a direct application to nonbelievers.

components.text: Explain how divine commands constitute duties for agents who neither apprehend the commands nor recognize the commander's authority.

response.rationale: The objection contacts the universality implication of the command account by distinguishing lack of obligation from mere lack of moral knowledge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It precisely targets the binding-authority component and states the alleged consequence for nonbelievers.

precisionFindings.rationale: Awareness of content, recognition of authority, obligation, and knowledge are carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The implication follows only if apprehension is necessary for authoritative binding, a premise asserted more than defended here.

charity.alternative: An authority can bind agents who fail to identify it, provided the requirement's content or authoritative character is otherwise accessible.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt emphasizes total nonapprehension but does not yet exclude indirect apprehension or objective jurisdiction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The implication is clear and consistent, but it depends on a material premise about apprehension as a condition of binding.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is strong, while support for the key authority premise is limited in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary universal-authority bridge at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection is carefully framed, but an important authority-without-identification alternative remains live.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that unrecognized commands fail to impose duties and explicitly separates this from lack of moral knowledge.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: An omniscient God would not prevent foreknown disobedience by issuing a command, but would add the evil of obligation violation, leaving the command's normative purpose unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: Wielenberg labels this his third challenge and sustains a single counterfactual argument about foreknown commands through its stated prediction.

components.text: Explain what necessary normative function a divine command serves when God foreknows it will not prevent the wrongful act.

response.rationale: The move directly questions command purpose by arguing that the command adds a violation without preventing the independently evil act.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the command-purpose demand through a concrete foreknowledge argument, though it assumes a prevention-focused rationale.

precisionFindings.rationale: The stipulated foreknowledge, added violation, prevention rationale, and resulting reason are distinctly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Foreknown nonprevention excludes one purpose but not communication, accountability, relationship, or just judgment.

charity.alternative: Commands may constitute accountability, communicate standards, or order relationships even when disobedience is foreknown.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection addresses prevention but does not exclude these nonpreventive purposes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The prevention argument is valid on its premise, but the broader unexplained-purpose conclusion risks a false dilemma.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment supports a limited question but not the exclusion of all alternative command functions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the rival's subsidiary command-rationale bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Its conclusion materially understates the strongest alternative rationales for issuing a foreknown-disobeyed command.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that the foreknown command cannot prevent the act and instead makes the wrongdoing include obligation violation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Divine commands can be the ultimate ground of duty within a hierarchy in which derivative moral principles and relevant circumstances determine obligations in particular cases.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly rejects Wielenberg's first challenge and explains his hierarchical account in a continuous first-person rebuttal.

components.text: Explain how promises, circumstances, and other morally relevant facts fit if divine commands remain the ultimate source of duty.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the plural-sources objection by placing derivative principles and situational facts within a hierarchy grounded in general commands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the uniqueness objection while preserving the acknowledged role of derivative moral considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: Ultimate source, derivative principles, general commands, and case-specific application are clearly differentiated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hierarchy is offered as a coherent compatibility answer, and the stated force is proportionate to that limited task.

charity.alternative: Plural morally relevant features may be independent grounds rather than merely derivative specifications of commands.
charity.decisiveQualification: The hierarchy accommodates their practical role but does not independently prove their derivative status.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The hierarchy coherently reconciles ultimate command grounding with derivative principles and contextual application.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The structure answers the compatibility objection, though it does not fully establish the asserted ultimate-source relation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-command bridge and its treatment of derivative principles.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply represents the pluralist concern accurately and supplies a fair answer, with one important grounding question remaining.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt places promises and other derivative facts beneath general commands in a hierarchy of obligation sources.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Nonbelievers remain subject to divine moral requirements because people can intuitively apprehend the content and authority of moral law without identifying God as its source.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig calls the nonbeliever challenge weak, states the Christian answer, and illustrates it with a complete no-trespassing analogy.

components.text: Explain how nonbelievers can be bound when they do not explicitly identify God as the source of the command.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes source identification from intuitive apprehension of a command's content and authority, directly answering the nonbeliever case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive scope premise with a clear distinction and an explanatory analogy.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-content-authority distinction is clear, though the claim that all people possess the intuition is broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal intuitive-access claim is stronger than the analogy and assertion supplied in the excerpt warrant.

charity.alternative: Some nonbelievers may apprehend moral content without apprehending that it carries a commander's authority.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply asserts intuitive authority as well as content but offers limited independent support for that extension.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction coherently blocks the inference from unknown source to absent obligation, with a broad accessibility premise remaining.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The fence analogy supports unknown-source authority, but the universal moral-analogy premise is insufficiently established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary universal-authority bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It squarely addresses the distinction, though difficult cases of impaired or absent authority apprehension remain.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt claims intuitive apprehension of moral content and authority despite failure to recognize those demands as God's commands.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: General divine commands establish culpability, retributive responsibility, and divine judgment, while divine-command theory itself does not require the disputed premise that God has middle knowledge.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly addresses the third challenge, identifies its alleged presupposition, and gives responsibility and judgment as his alternative rationale.

components.text: Identify a nonpreventive purpose for issuing general commands despite foreknown disobedience.

response.rationale: The reply supplies culpability, retributive responsibility, and judgment as command functions and separates divine-command theory from middle knowledge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the decisive purpose demand with several explicit nonpreventive functions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The independence from middle knowledge and the accountability function of general commands are clearly delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The response establishes a possible purpose, but saying judgment is impossible without commands presupposes the disputed duty theory.

charity.alternative: Agents might be accountable for independently grounded duties without a divine command adding a distinct violation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply assumes commands are necessary for culpability rather than separately defending that necessity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The nonpreventive rationale is coherent, though the necessity of commands for responsibility risks circularity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The distinction from middle knowledge is supported, while the claimed dependence of justice on commands is asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary command-purpose bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It answers the stated challenge but leaves the rival's independent-accountability alternative insufficiently addressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt disclaims middle knowledge as essential and says general commands enable responsibility, retribution, and divine judgment.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Observed cognitive reliability can justify confidence in evolved faculties despite speculative arguments that unguided evolution probably produces unreliable cognition.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage follows Wielenberg’s direct discussion of Craig and Plantinga and presents a first-person analogy within his uninterrupted rebuttal.

components.text: Explain why naturalism and unguided evolution do not defeat justified confidence in broadly reliable cognitive faculties.

response.rationale: The reply appeals to observed reliability and compares speculative evolutionary skepticism to armchair doubts about a repeatedly reliable instrument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive defeater claim, though it does not fully analyze the conditional probabilities behind that claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The experiential rebuttal is clear, but reliability shifts between believers, beliefs, and cognitive faculties generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is framed as reasonableness, appropriately matching the defeater-rebuttal evidence supplied.

charity.alternative: The evolutionary defeater may challenge the trustworthiness of the very observations invoked to establish reliability.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy does not fully answer this alleged epistemic circularity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Observed success can rebut generalized skepticism, but the lighter analogy leaves the possible circularity materially unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Empirical reliability is a relevant warrant, though no representative evolutionary evidence or probability comparison is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central evolutionary reliability objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly contests speculative probability claims but omits a decisive self-referential feature of the strongest objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses a reliable-lighter analogy and argues that accepted naturalism permits belief in mostly reliable evolved believers.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.proposition: Godless normative realism is supported as an inference to the best explanation of objective moral facts after competing accounts are comparatively considered.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Wielenberg, who answers in the first person and explicitly describes the reasoning supporting his own metaethical theory.

response.rationale: This constructive move proposes inference to the best explanation as the overall support structure for godless normative realism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It provides a direct comparative method, though the selected span does not complete the alternative comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly labels its method as a loose inference to the best explanation of objective moral facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The methodological claim is appropriately cautious, but the excerpt does not display the comparative evidence needed for a best explanation.
